normalized.governing_thought: Don't give exclusivity away before it is earned: sign a nonexclusive OEM pilot now and make North American exclusivity conditional on certification and audited volumes
executive_summary: Recommendation: Decline Option X as drafted. Sign Option N, a 12-month nonexclusive pilot at $350 per robot, and agree up front the gates under which Option M (limited exclusivity) takes effect: certification passed, two audited quarters at about 9,000 robots a year, and contract protections signed.
1 The deal is worth less than it is being presented as

The $2.0M is a recoupable advance, not extra revenue: three-year OEM cash is $8.7M, not $10.7M. After $80/robot support, $0.9M/yr engineering, the $0.45M assessment and displaced direct sales, exclusivity is worth +$2.2M to +$2.8M at plan but only −$0.04M to +$0.55M at 65% volumes.
2 The evidence the board requires for irreversible exclusivity does not exist yet

Lab uptime is 98.8% against a 99.5% production bar. The third-party assessment has not started. OEM volumes are unaudited, and the 14,000 'booked devices' are a forecast. The growth claim rests on correlation. The draft lacks audit rights, a royalty floor, release triggers and code escrow.
3 The phased N→M structure beats every alternative

It earns $50 more per robot, keeps the direct channel (~$1.48M of gross margin on new ARR in 2028), and matches X's value even if the OEM ships 24–32% fewer robots. It holds cash at least $0.55M above the $2.6M buffer in the worst case, and it fails none of the board's conditions.
4 Gates, signposts and next steps make the decision reversible

Start the $0.45M assessment now; it is on the critical path for every OEM route. Convert to exclusivity only after certification and audited shipments of at least 2,250 robots a quarter. If the OEM insists on exclusivity at signing, walk away and fall back to direct sales plus the integration-firm pilot.

slides.title: Of six conditions that would have to hold for exclusivity at signing to be right, only one partly holds, so the 'don't sign yet' hypothesis stands

claims.claim: Initial hypothesis: Boreal should not grant exclusivity at signing; a nonexclusive or milestone deal captures the OEM upside without giving up the direct channel.
1. The $2.0M signing payment adds value on top of royalties — Does not hold
evidence: It is an advance credited against the first $2.0M of royalties, and the partner can demand an offset. 3-yr cash is $8.7M either way

claims.claim: 2. Exclusivity creates value even in the low case and with realistic channel overlap — Partly: plan case only
evidence: +$2.2–2.8M at plan; −$0.04M to +$0.55M at 65% volumes with Sales' 30–70% overlap

claims.claim: 3. The product is production-ready in the OEM's hardware — Does not hold
evidence: 98.8% lab uptime vs 99.5% required; no loaded-warehouse or collision-heavy test; assessment not started

claims.claim: 4. OEM volumes and the growth story are reliable enough to commit on — Does not hold
evidence: Shipments unaudited; '14,000 booked devices' have no purchase orders; competitor evidence is correlational

claims.claim: 5. Exclusivity is the only way to win the OEM's volume — Does not hold
evidence: The OEM will consider Option N (nonexclusive, $350/robot) and Option M (gated exclusivity)

claims.claim: 6. The contract protects Boreal if forecasts or certification miss — Does not hold
evidence: No audit right, no royalty floor after the advance, no release triggers, no code escrow

claims.claim: The hypothesis survives, refined. The problem is exclusivity before evidence, not exclusivity itself, so the answer is a gated path to exclusivity rather than a flat 'no'.

slides.title: The $2.0M is an advance on royalties, not extra revenue: three-year OEM cash is $8.7M, not the $10.7M the 'revenue win' framing implies

claims.claim: Total cash always equals royalties earned; the advance is cash received early, then netted out of 2028 royalty cash
evidence: Plan 2027: 5,000 robots; royalties 1.50; advance credit −1.50; royalty cash 0.00; total OEM cash 2.00

claims.claim: Revenue = royalties earned as qualifying robots ship and payment is collected: $1.5M in 2027 at plan, not $3.5M.
The $2.0M is a minimum-guarantee liability until it is earned. The partner can demand an offset if guaranteed performance is missed.
The 'revenue win plus recurring royalties' framing double-counts $2.0M, overstating 3-year OEM income by 23%
What the advance buys: timing only. It brings $1.5–2.0M of cash forward into 2027, which Boreal does not need to stay above its buffer
In the stress case, 2028 royalty cash falls to $0.93M because $1.03M of credit is still being recouped.

slides.title: After full costs, $3.00M of 2028 plan royalties shrinks to about $0.56M of incremental value, 19% rather than the dashboard's 100%

claims.claim: 2028 plan royalties shrink to ~$0.56M incremental value after costs (waterfall)
evidence: Variable support (10,000 × $80): 0.8
OEM-specific engineering: 0.9
OEM contribution: 1.3
Displaced direct gross margin: 0.738
Incremental value: 0.562

claims.claim: CFO dashboard: 100% margin. It counts only the $300 royalty.
Per robot: $220 (73%) after $80 of support, before any fixed cost.
Complete incremental view: ~19% at plan.
evidence: $0.27–0.86M across 30–70% overlap

claims.claim: At 65% volumes it turns negative
Exclusivity bars all new direct North American licences, including customers who buy other OEMs' robots. That forgone margin is a real cost of Option X, not of the OEM channel in general.
evidence: Lost direct margin = 50% (midpoint of Sales' 30–70% overlap) × $1.8M ARR × 82% gross margin

slides.title: Over 2027–29, exclusivity is worth +$2.2–2.8M at plan volumes but only −$0.04M to +$0.55M if the OEM ships 65% of plan

claims.claim: A. Direct cohort counted in 2028 only: Even on the most favourable reading, the low case leaves at most $0.55M of value for three years of irreversible exclusivity.
B. If direct ARR renews, as recurring revenue normally does, the low case destroys up to $1.1M at Sales' 70% overlap.
Costs assume full-year engineering from 2027, which is conservative. If deployments start late in 2027, all OEM options gain equally and the ranking does not change.

slides.title: Exclusivity breaks even only if the OEM ships 6,100–8,800 robots a year; the 65% case (6,500 in 2028) barely clears the most optimistic end

claims.claim: At Sales' 30–70% overlap, the hurdle is 6,100–8,800 robots a year. The plan (10,000) clears it; the stress case (6,500) clears only the 30% end.
evidence: Breakeven, 0% overlap: 4,091
OEM 2028 65% stress: 6,500
OEM 2028 partner plan: 10,000
Breakeven = ($0.9M + overlap × $1.476M) ÷ ($300 − $80)

claims.claim: Option M's proposed gate of 5,000 annualised is below every realistic breakeven. It should rise to about 9,000 (2,250 per quarter) unless the scope excludes customers on other OEMs' robots.
Under Option N, the OEM programme alone breaks even at 3,333 robots, and the direct channel is untouched.

evidence: Nov 2026: assessment not started
Apr 2027: board meets; under X, exclusivity binds here

claims.claim: The board requires documented uptime and safety validation in OEM hardware before irreversible exclusivity. Option X fails that condition by design.
Production deployment cannot start until the assessment is complete, so the 2027 plan of 5,000 robots is at risk, and with it the advance's offset exposure.
The gap is closable but unproven

about 24 → 10 hours per robot over the 12-week trial

slides.title: The upside case rests on unaudited volumes, an untested 'fully incremental' claim and a correlational competitor analogy

claims.claim: OEM volumes are a forecast, not a commitment
evidence: Quarterly shipment data are not independently audited, and the draft contract has no audit right
The '14,000 booked devices' have no purchase orders
The 2027 forecast of 5,000 assumes production shipments in a year when certification lands in September at the earliest
Impact: plan → 65% moves 3-yr value by −$2.2M

claims.claim: Channel overlap is unknown, and it drives the answer
evidence: CEO says 0% overlap; Sales says 30–70%
Neither view is backed by customer-level identifiers
Each 10 points of overlap is worth ~$0.15M a year of displaced direct gross margin ($1.8M × 82% × 10%)
Impact: 30% → 70% moves the breakeven from 6,100 to 8,800 robots/yr

claims.claim: The overlap can be measured during a nonexclusive pilot. It cannot be measured after exclusivity has closed the direct channel.
'Exclusivity caused competitors' growth' is not shown
evidence: Five competitors' exclusive OEM deals coincided with faster growth. That is a correlation.
Those firms had more marketing support, more mature products and higher market share before they signed
No causal evidence is available, so we give this argument zero weight in the economics
Impact: no evidence that exclusivity itself adds volume over N

slides.title: As drafted, the contract leaves Boreal exposed on six terms, and its scope blocks the growing direct channel

claims.claim: Audit rights: no clear right to audit reported shipments
evidence: Required: independent, shipment-level audit right; quarterly reports reconciled to invoices

claims.claim: Royalty floor: none once the $2.0M advance is used up
evidence: Required: annual minimum royalty; exclusivity lapses automatically if missed

claims.claim: Release triggers: no automatic release
evidence: Required: automatic release on model retirement, certification slip or missed minimums

claims.claim: IP protection: source code delivered as freely reusable OEM IP
evidence: Required: source code escrow with narrow release conditions; no IP transfer

claims.claim: Scope: all new North American sales, including customers on other OEMs' robots — chief strategic opportunity cost
evidence: ~$1.48M/yr of direct margin at risk
Required: limit to the OEM's robot series; carve out existing and other-OEM customers

claims.claim: Guarantee offset: the $2.0M can claw back, e.g. if certification delays 2027 shipments
evidence: Required: define the offset; cap it at the unearned balance; no offset for OEM-driven shortfalls

claims.claim: Existing direct contracts cannot be terminated for convenience. Any exclusivity must apply only to future new North American robot sales, or Boreal faces unquantified contract claims.

slides.title: Recommendation: sign Option N now and pre-agree three gates that switch on limited exclusivity (Option M) once certification and audited volumes show it pays

claims.claim: Phase 0 (Now → Apr 2027) Prepare
evidence: Commission the $0.45M third-party security and safety assessment now
Negotiate the N term sheet with the M gates pre-agreed
Tag customers so OEM/direct overlap can be measured

claims.claim: Phase 1 (Apr 2027 → ~Q1 2028) Option N: nonexclusive pilot
evidence: 12 months, $350 per shipped robot, no advance
Boreal keeps all direct and other-OEM rights
Audit rights and monthly royalty reports from day one
Existing licences untouched

claims.claim: Phase 2 (Earliest ~Q2 2028) Option M: limited exclusivity
evidence: New North American sales of the OEM's robot series only
Up to 3 years, with an annual minimum royalty
Automatic release if minimums are missed, the model is retired or certification lapses
Termination payment ≥ 1 year of displaced direct margin (~$1.5M)

claims.claim: All three gates must be passed before Phase 2. Each is verifiable by the board, not by OEM assertion.
evidence: Gate 1 Certification: ≥ 99.5% uptime in OEM production hardware in a fully loaded warehouse, including collision-heavy peaks; documented safe-stop; third-party assessment passed

Gate 2 Verified demand: two consecutive audited quarters of ≥ 2,250 robots (~9,000/yr), at or above breakeven at 70% overlap (8,787 robots/yr). Accept the OEM's 5,000/yr gate only if other-OEM customers are carved out
Gate 3 Contract protections: audit right, post-advance royalty floor, automatic release triggers, source code escrow, existing and other-OEM customers carved out, defined offset terms

slides.title: Negotiate by trading price, scope and timing for evidence, and walk away from any form of exclusivity that binds at signing

Independent shipment audit right
Source code escrow; no transfer of reusable IP
Automatic release on model retirement or certification slip

claims.claim: Tradeables (give to get)
evidence: Royalty: concede from $350 toward $300 at conversion in return for a royalty floor
Volume gate: accept 5,000/yr instead of ~9,000 if the scope excludes other-OEM customers

Term: shorter initial exclusivity (e.g. 2 years) with renewal on performance
An advance at conversion, structured as a capped and clearly defined guarantee

evidence: Continue direct sales: ~$1.8M new ARR in 2028, ~$1.48M gross margin
Take the integration firm's nonexclusive 1,200-robot pilot ($0.22M support budget, no guarantee)
Complete certification anyway; return to the OEM with production evidence
This loses the OEM's upside (+$2.2–2.8M at plan) but avoids the low-case downside

claims.claim: Boreal's leverage is limited, but the OEM has itself put Options N and M on the table, and Boreal has not yet committed its IP.
Messaging: announce a 'strategic OEM partnership' now. Report any advance as a recoupable guarantee, never as revenue.

evidence: Today: $80 estimate

normalized.recommendation: Decline Option X as drafted. Sign Option N, a 12-month nonexclusive pilot at $350 per robot, and agree up front the gates under which Option M (limited exclusivity) takes effect: certification passed, two audited quarters at about 9,000 robots a year, and contract protections signed. alternatives_considered.treatment: Reject as drafted: +$2.2–2.8M plan; −$0.04 to +$0.55M at 65%; weak low-case resilience (thin margin, offset exposure); no reversibility (3 years, binding at signing); fails the validation-first condition; lowest deal risk as it is the OEM's ask.

Recommend: phase 1. Up to +$4.7M plan / +$1.9M at 65% if terms hold (upper bound); $270/robot, no guarantee to recoup; high reversibility; meets all board conditions; medium deal risk as price not guaranteed.
Recommend: phase 2. X-like upside taken only once proven; gates screen out the low case; meets all conditions; medium deal risk, termination payment still open.
Fallback: keeps ~$1.48M/yr direct margin on 2028 new ARR; no OEM upside; forgoes the OEM.
Fallback if N refused: as direct, less the $0.45M assessment; high deal risk as OEM may choose another supplier.
A complement to N and to the fallbacks; X would likely bar it; royalty terms not in the pack, not valued.
